title: Krasheninnikov, Kamchatka
subtitle: Follow real radar-scattering changes beside NASA’s volcano time-lapse

references.title: NASA’s Krasheninnikov time-lapse and dated frames
references.description: Official 17-date HH L-band NISAR visualization, December 2025 to August 2026. Our five observations match its late-season dates; this is a qualitative reference, not a georeferenced lava mask or peer-reviewed validation paper.

references.title: NASA/JPL explains the spreading lava field

references.title: Smithsonian eruption chronology and volcano location
references.description: Independent GVP/KVERT reports provide eruption context. Activity began before our June baseline; this is chronology, not a supplied flow boundary.

question: What changed in radar scattering around Krasheninnikov between June and August 2026?
method: Use the five compatible descending-track HH observations on a 20 m local UTM grid. Screen native samples before averaging linear gamma-zero power, then convert to dB. Clip grid cell centres to the selected geographic rectangle and compare only cells usable on every selected date. Subtract the 18 June observed baseline. Smooth each signed departure with normalized Gaussian sigma 40 m while retaining missing cells. Separately retain positive and negative four-connected patches meeting ±3 dB and at least 30,000 m². Map the latest change, first observed qualifying date and same-sign change on consecutive later observations. No spatial reference rectangle, independent lava boundary, optical snow mask or wetness model is used.
expected: The recorded run has 478.0604 km² of shared usable support; 145.6028 km² of latest brightness-change candidates, including 128.2920 km² repeated on consecutive later acquisitions. These are scattering-change areas, not lava areas. Bright crater and finger-like eastern-flow structures are recognizable in acquired HH images, but much of the existing flow field predates the baseline.
interpret: Start with the latest smoothed departure in dB: red is increased radar brightness and blue decreased brightness, not hot and cold lava. Changed patches apply the saved threshold/area rules; repeated evidence describes sampled dates, not continuous activity. Explore time shows acquired HH brightness with one shared automatic scale. Compare those snapshots with NASA’s dated images to recognize the crater and existing flow field. A stable bright flow can show little change, while snowmelt or wetness elsewhere can produce a strong departure. First-change indices have a date key; they do not establish the exact emplacement time.
limits: This is a qualitative surface-scattering case study, not a validated lava-boundary map or an exact reproduction of NASA’s display. The June baseline already contains lava. Snowmelt, wetness and terrain effects contribute broad changes; P06 does not classify them separately or identify temperature, magma, volume or deformation. NASA uses an oblique 3D view and stated 10 m imagery; our north-up analysis uses 20 m cells and 40 m smoothing sigma. Exact source geometry and display processing cannot be certified from NASA’s video. No independent dated lava polygons were used, so precision, recall, IoU and lava-area accuracy are not reported. Missing dates are unobserved, including the 24-day final gap.

visual_comparison_note: The NASA panel is published reference imagery. Our continuous departure map answers what changed since June, not where all lava exists. The separate acquired-HH strip explains why a flow can remain visible while its departure is small. Compare morphology and dates qualitatively; perspective, spatial support and processing differ. Snowmelt and wetness are not independently separated in this version.

evidence.label: Qualitative scattering comparison
evidence.description: The real radar changes are reproducible, but this example does not establish lava detection; seasonal and wetness changes remain mixed with volcanic surface effects.
evidence.transfer_validation: Not established on an independently held-out event or region.

comparison_review.conclusion: The real radar changes are reproducible, but this example does not establish lava detection; seasonal and wetness changes remain mixed with volcanic surface effects.
agrees: Five selected late-season dates correspond to NASA’s June–August sequence.
Acquired HH imagery contains recognizable flow/crater morphology alongside the published frames.
differs: NASA displays oblique 3D brightness imagery across 17 dates; our north-up change map compares five dates against an already-erupting June baseline.
Our 20 m grid and 40 m smoothing differ from NASA’s stated display; existing lava can remain bright without showing a new departure.
unverified: No independent dated flow polygons: no lava precision, recall, IoU or lava-area estimate.
Snowmelt, wetness and terrain effects are not independently separated. First radar change is not eruption onset.
comparison_review.next_check: Independently georeferenced dated flow boundaries and optical/thermal or snow/wetness evidence.
